note: REVISES the earlier live-triage note below, which was wrong. At 18:37 I told Jarvis the no-go was trusting a noisy hour-ahead forecast bucket over Open-Meteo's live nowcast (18:30: 84%/84%, 'looks beautiful'). The actual outcome was the opposite: the nowcast was the misleading read, stale by the time of sunset, and the hour-ahead forecast correctly caught a fast-incoming deck the nowcast had no way to see coming -- a nowcast is a snapshot with no lead time; a short-range forecast model assimilating recent radar/satellite can sometimes catch an approaching feature a nowcast cannot. No code was changed based on the live triage (deliberately -- 'not on one night'), so nothing needs reverting. JW, 2026-10-16: don't switch to preferring nowcast based on tonight; if anything tonight argues for the hour-ahead bucket. Treat as confirmation the existing no-go logic should NOT move. Photo viewed directly 2026-10-16: near-unbroken low gray deck (~90-95%), one narrow gold sliver at the horizon, no color on the clouds -- matches JW's own 'at most a D' call and the model's F. Independent confirmation, not just taking the description on faith. SECOND PHOTO (5 min later, looking further left), per Jarvis: towering cumulus wall, broken blue-gray gaps, clean orange horizon band -- but cloud BASES unlit, flat gray not pink/gold. JW: 'still beautiful but it's covering the sunset... a little to the left you can see it would have been beautiful.' So: F was right for the direct light path to the sun; the broader scene (JW's own estimate, 'maybe a C') had real structure that never got painted. This is the SAME distinction the Horizon leaf already scores separately for distant cloud (shape vs. light-path/'block' -- server.js h35-shape/h35-block), just not something the site's own overhead sky (Clouds/site-view) currently asks. Worth considering for later: see CLAUDE.md. Not implemented -- one evening, two photos, is not grounds to add a metric. CORRECTED by JW directly (not Jarvis's paraphrase): 'This is not a C. This could be an A if the sun were some number of degrees to the left.' So the SCENE was A-grade structure -- the cumulus wall, gaps and clean horizon band were genuinely excellent -- and the sunset itself was F purely because of GEOMETRY: the sun set behind the solid part of the deck, a few degrees from a gap that was right there. This is sharper than 'shape vs light-path' (the earlier framing in this note) -- it's specifically whether a gap sits ALONG THE SUN'S AZIMUTH at the moment of the event, not overall coverage or even overall light-path blockage. JW's own suggestion: direction (cloud cover along the sun's bearing vs a few degrees off it) may matter more than aggregate coverage. See CLAUDE.md -- this strengthens, and is likely the same root cause as, the existing open Horizon-leaf limitation (fixed-distance sampling, no fine angular resolution around the sun's bearing). Caveat: cloud_cover fields from the weather models are AREAL fractions per grid cell, not angularly-resolved -- there may be no data source available that can tell 'is there a gap exactly where the sun is' with the precision this would need, which is a real limit on what can be done here even with the right idea. ANOTHER IDEA FROM JW: coverage alone shouldn't decide the no-go -- 'if the sky is 80-90% cumulus and interesting and textured, that's really different than if it's 90% flat solid.' Textured/cellular cloud at high coverage can still be a great scene; flat stratus at the same coverage is dead. This maps DIRECTLY onto existing code: server.js already has a CAPE-based texture leaf ('Texture (CAPE)', weight 0.08 inside Clouds), explicitly commented 'experimental ... light weight, here to play with over time' -- but it is NOT consulted by detectNoGo's Socked-in check, which only looks at total/low coverage. Tonight's actual reading: Home's texture leaf read CAPE 23 J/kg, 'slab-prone' -- consistent with photo 1's flat deck, but photo 2 (different part of the sky) showed a visible convective cumulus tower the single grid-cell CAPE sample didn't capture. So the idea is right in principle but the existing signal's resolution may itself be too coarse to fully deliver on it -- a real atmosphere isn't homogeneous across one site's sky the way a single sampled CAPE value assumes. NOT implemented: promoting an admittedly-experimental, lightly-weighted signal to gate a hard F needs its own validation first (CLAUDE.md's own bar), not a same-night change. Jarvis also floated, independently, a fixed west-facing camera + vision model on JW's spare GPU as continuous ground truth (gap-on-sun, lit/unlit bases, texture vs flat) -- can't forecast but could calibrate continuously. Explicitly JW's call whether to pursue.

This is the SECOND confirmed instance of the same unresolved idea flagged 2026-10-16 (CLAUDE.md, 'coverage alone shouldn't decide the no-go... textured/cellular cloud at high coverage can still be a great scene') and not implemented there because 'one evening is not grounds to add a metric.' Per CLAUDE.md's own evidence bar (check a finding against a second, differently-drawn sample before acting), this finding has now survived a second, independent check on a different night with a different mechanism (CAPE/far-band gradient this time, not a second photo of the same sky) and points at the same fix: the no-go should look past raw site-level total/low coverage when texture or the band gradient suggests the deck isn't uniform.
